title: OLS diagnostics
dek: Residuals, leverage, and influence are how you see whether the projection you computed is a scientific fit or a hostage to one row.
story: A residual eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ is not yet a diagnostic. Scale it. A standardised residual uses σ̂ √(1−hᵢᵢ) in the denominator because a high-leverage point is expected to have a smaller raw residual. Studentised residuals leave observation i out of σ̂.

Leverage hᵢᵢ flags unusual x. Cook’s distance and DFBETAS flag influence on β̂ — a point can have a small residual and still move a slope if it sits far out in x. In MIC-by-dose plots, the highest dose often is both.

QQ plots of residuals check Gaussianity of e, which you need for exact t, not for BLUE. Residual-versus-fitted and scale-location plots check curvature and heteroskedasticity, which you need for the mean and the SEs. Do not run a 12-plot ritual without a sentence.
deepTitle: Leave-one-out and what to do next
deep: Hat: hᵢᵢ = xᵢᵀ (XᵀX)⁻¹ xᵢ. Rule of thumb hᵢᵢ > 2p/n is a flag, not a theorem. In designed experiments with replication, leverages are often equal by construction — diagnostics then move to residual plots.
Cook’s Dᵢ ∝ hᵢᵢ eᵢ² / (1−hᵢᵢ)². Large D means β̂_{(−i)} moved. Report whether the scientific conclusion (sign, interval excluding 0) moved, not only whether D exceeded 4/n.

If residual plots show a curve, the linear mean is wrong — transform Y, add a term, or leave OLS. If they show a fan, the spherical-error SE is wrong — sandwich, WLS, or a GLM variance function. If one isolate owns the slope, that is a data-point problem, not a software option.
GLM Pearson and deviance residuals are the analogues. High-leverage binary points (complete separation) break MLEs rather than just Cook’s D. Diagnostics do not stop at Gaussian OLS.

visual.caption: Schematic diagnostic signatures. Left: one high-leverage isolate. Middle: a fan (heteroskedasticity). Right: a curved mean. These are different failures; they do not share one fix.

example.title: One high-dose isolate
example.setup: OLS of log MIC on dose, n = 18. Seventeen points in dose 0–2. One isolate at dose 10 with a moderate residual. Default slope is steep. Leave that row out and the slope halves.

steps.title: Compute h and D
steps.body: The dose-10 row will have large hᵢᵢ. Even a modest eᵢ can make Dᵢ huge because of the (1−h)² denominator.

steps.title: Scientific fork
steps.body: If dose 10 is a protocol-valid observation, keep it and perhaps use a nonlinear mean or robust regression, and report sensitivity. If it is a mis-labelled dilution, it is not a data point.

steps.title: Do not average the two slopes
steps.body: The two fits are answering different questions (with versus without that design point). Write both, plus the residual plot, in the supplement. That is diagnostics as science, not as a delete-outliers ritual.

example.takeaway: Influence is a sensitivity analysis. Deleting in silence is not.

choices: The point is unusual in covariate space and can own its fitted value
check.answer: The point is unusual in covariate space and can own its fitted value
check.why: hᵢᵢ is a property of x, not of y. Residuals can be small at high leverage; that is when influence is sneaky.

whyWrong.The residual must be large: High h actually tends to shrink |e|.

check.prompt: If hᵢᵢ = 0.5, σ̂ = 2, eᵢ = 1, the standardised residual rᵢ = eᵢ/(σ̂√(1−hᵢᵢ)) is:

whyWrong.1: That ignores both σ̂ and leverage.

check.prompt: On the diagnostic small-multiples, why are leverage, fan, and curve separate panels?
check.figureHint: Three titled panels with different bar patterns.
choices: Because one robust SE fixes all three
Because they are different failures of the OLS story (x-space, variance, mean) and need different next moves
Because Cook’s D is a likelihood
check.answer: Because they are different failures of the OLS story (x-space, variance, mean) and need different next moves
check.why: The plate is a triage board. Do not collapse it into “check residuals.”

whyWrong.Because one robust SE fixes all three: Sandwich does not fix a curved mean or a bogus point.
